q: Which of the following techniques cannot be used to determine the minimum inhibitory concentration of an antimicrobial drug against a particular microbe?
why: The correct answer is: Kirby-Bauer disk diffusion test. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: The utility of an antibiogram is that it shows antimicrobial susceptibility trends
why: The correct answer is: in a localized population.. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: Which of the following has yielded compounds with the most antimicrobial activity?
why: The correct answer is: soil. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: Which of the following would be a sign of an infection?
why: The correct answer is: fever. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: Which of the following is an example of a noncommunicable infectious disease?
options: food poisoning due to a preformed bacterial toxin in food
skin infection acquired from a dog bite
infection acquired from the stick of a contaminated needle
why: The correct answer is: food poisoning due to a preformed bacterial toxin in food. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: During an oral surgery, the surgeon nicked the patient’s gum with a sharp instrument. This allowed Streptococcus, a bacterium normally present in the mouth, to gain access to the blood. As a result, the patient developed bacterial endocarditis (an infection of the heart). Which type of disease is this?
why: The correct answer is: iatrogenic. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: Which period is the stage of disease during which the patient begins to present general signs and symptoms?
why: The correct answer is: prodromal. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: A communicable disease that can be easily transmitted from person to person is which type of disease?
why: The correct answer is: contagious. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

card.q: A person steps on a rusty nail and develops tetanus. In this case, the person has acquired a(n) __________ disease.

q: Which of the following is a pathogen that could not be identified by the original Koch’s postulates?
why: The correct answer is: Human immunodeficiency virus. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: Pathogen A has an ID₅₀ of 50 particles, pathogen B has an ID₅₀ of 1,000 particles, and pathogen C has an ID₅₀ of 1 × 10⁶ particles. Which pathogen is most virulent?
why: The correct answer is: pathogen A. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: Which of the following choices lists the steps of pathogenesis in the correct order?
why: The correct answer is: exposure, adhesion, invasion, infection. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

card.q: A(n) __________ pathogen causes disease only when conditions are favorable for the microorganism because of transfer to an inappropriate body site or weakened immunity in an individual.

q: Which of the following would be a virulence factor of a pathogen?
options: a surface protein allowing the pathogen to bind to host cells
a secondary host the pathogen can infect
a surface protein the host immune system recognizes
the ability to form a provirus
why: The correct answer is: a surface protein allowing the pathogen to bind to host cells. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: You have recently identified a new toxin. It is produced by a gram-negative bacterium. It is composed mostly of protein, has high toxicity, and is not heat stable. You also discover that it targets liver cells. Based on these characteristics, how would you classify this toxin?
why: The correct answer is: exotoxin. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: Which of the following applies to hyaluronidase?
options: It acts as a spreading factor.
It is an example of an adhesin.
It is produced by immune cells to target pathogens.
why: The correct answer is: It acts as a spreading factor.. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: Phospholipases are enzymes that do which of the following?
options: promote pathogen spread through connective tissue.
degrade nucleic acid to promote spread of pathogen
degrade cell membranes to allow pathogens to escape phagosomes
why: The correct answer is: degrade cell membranes to allow pathogens to escape phagosomes. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

card.q: Adhesins are usually located on __________ of the pathogen and are composed mainly of __________ and __________.
The Shiga and diphtheria toxins target __________ in host cells.

Antigenic __________ is the result of reassortment of genes responsible for the production of influenza virus spike proteins between different virus particles while in the same host, whereas antigenic __________ is the result of point mutations in the spike proteins.

q: Which of the following is a major virulence factor for the fungal pathogen Cryptococcus?
why: The correct answer is: capsule. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: Which of the following pathogens undergoes antigenic variation to avoid immune defenses?
why: The correct answer is: Plasmodium. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

card.q: Candida can invade tissue by producing the exoenzymes __________ and __________.

Match each term with its description. ___sporadic disease A. the number of disease cases per 100,000 individuals ___endemic disease B. a disease in higher than expected numbers around the world ___pandemic disease C. the number of deaths from a disease for every 10,000 individuals ___morbidity rate D. a disease found occasionally in a region with cases occurring mainly in isolation from each other ___mortality rate E. a disease found regularly in a region
The ________ collects data and conducts epidemiologic studies in the United States.
card.a: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, or CDC

card.q: ________occurs when an infected individual passes the infection on to other individuals, who pass it on to still others, increasing the penetration of the infection into the susceptible population.
A batch of food contaminated with botulism exotoxin, consumed at a family reunion by most of the members of a family, would be an example of a ________ outbreak.

q: Which is the most common type of biological vector of human disease?
why: The correct answer is: arthropods. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: A mosquito bites a person who subsequently develops a fever and abdominal rash. What type of transmission would this be?
why: The correct answer is: biological vector transmission. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: Cattle are allowed to pasture in a field that contains the farmhouse well, and the farmer’s family becomes ill with a gastrointestinal pathogen after drinking the water. What type of transmission of infectious agents would this be?
why: The correct answer is: vehicle transmission. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: A blanket from a child with chickenpox is likely to be contaminated with the virus that causes chickenpox (Varicella-zoster virus). What is the blanket called?
why: The correct answer is: fomite. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

card.q: A patient in the hospital with a urinary catheter develops a bladder infection. This is an example of a(n) ________ infection.

q: Which of the following would NOT be considered an emerging disease?
why: The correct answer is: Tuberculosis. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: Which of the following would NOT be considered a reemerging disease?
why: The correct answer is: West Nile virus fever/encephalitis. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: Which of the following factors can lead to reemergence of a disease?
options: A mutation that allows it to infect humans
A period of decline in vaccination rates
A change in disease reporting procedures
Better education on the signs and symptoms of the disease
why: The correct answer is: A period of decline in vaccination rates. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: Why are emerging diseases with very few cases the focus of intense scrutiny?
options: They tend to be more deadly
They are increasing and therefore not controlled
They naturally have higher transmission rates
They occur more in developed countries
why: The correct answer is: They are increasing and therefore not controlled. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

card.q: The ________ collects data and conducts epidemiologic studies at the global level.

q: Which of the following best describes the innate nonspecific immune system?
options: a targeted and highly specific response to a single pathogen or molecule
a generalized and nonspecific set of defenses against a class or group of pathogens
a set of barrier mechanisms that adapts to specific pathogens after repeated exposure
the production of antibody molecules against pathogens
why: The correct answer is: a generalized and nonspecific set of defenses against a class or group of pathogens. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: Which of the following constantly sheds dead cells along with any microbes that may be attached to those cells?
why: The correct answer is: epidermis. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: Which of the following uses a particularly dense suite of tight junctions to prevent microbes from entering the underlying tissue?
why: The correct answer is: the blood-brain barrier. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

card.q: The muscular contraction of the intestines that results in movement of material through the digestive tract is called ________.

q: Which of the following serve as chemical signals between cells and stimulate a wide range of nonspecific defenses?
why: The correct answer is: cytokines. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: Bacteriocins and defensins are types of which of the following?
why: The correct answer is: antimicrobial peptides. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: Which of the following chemical mediators is secreted onto the surface of the skin?
why: The correct answer is: sebum. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: Identify the complement activation pathway that is triggered by the binding of an acute-phase protein to a pathogen.
why: The correct answer is: lectin. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: Histamine, leukotrienes, prostaglandins, and bradykinin are examples of which of the following?
options: chemical mediators primarily found in the digestive system
antimicrobial peptides found on the skin
why: The correct answer is: chemical mediators that promote inflammation. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

card.q: ________ are antimicrobial peptides produced by members of the normal microbiota.
The process by which cells are drawn or attracted to an area by a microbe invader is known as ________.

q: White blood cells are also referred to as which of the following?
why: The correct answer is: leukocytes. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: Hematopoiesis occurs in which of the following?
why: The correct answer is: bone marrow. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: Granulocytes are which type of cell?
why: The correct answer is: leukocyte. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

card.q: Platelets are also called ________.
The cell in the bone marrow that gives rise to all other blood cell types is the ________.
PMNs are another name for ________.
Kupffer cells residing in the liver are a type of ________.
_____________ are similar to basophils, but reside in tissues rather than circulating in the blood.

q: PAMPs would be found on the surface of which of the following?
why: The correct answer is: pathogen. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: ________ on phagocytes bind to PAMPs on bacteria, which triggers the uptake and destruction of the bacterial pathogens?
why: The correct answer is: PRRs. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: Which of the following best characterizes the mode of pathogen recognition for opsonin-dependent phagocytosis?
options: Opsonins produced by a pathogen attract phagocytes through chemotaxis.
A PAMP on the pathogen’s surface is recognized by a phagocyte’s toll-like receptors.
A pathogen is first coated with a molecule such as a complement protein, which allows it to be recognized by phagocytes.
A pathogen is coated with a molecule such as a complement protein that immediately lyses the cell.
why: The correct answer is: A pathogen is first coated with a molecule such as a complement protein, which allows it to be recognized by phagocytes.. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

card.q: ________, also known as diapedesis, refers to the exit from the bloodstream of neutrophils and other circulating leukocytes.
Toll-like receptors are examples of ________.

q: Which refers to swelling as a result of inflammation?
why: The correct answer is: edema. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: Which type of inflammation occurs at the site of an injury or infection?
why: The correct answer is: acute. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

card.q: A(n) ________ is a walled-off area of infected tissue that exhibits chronic inflammation.
The ________ is the part of the body responsible for regulating body temperature.

q: Antibodies are produced by ________.
why: The correct answer is: plasma cells. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: Cellular adaptive immunity is carried out by ________.
why: The correct answer is: T cells. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: A single antigen molecule may be composed of many individual ________.
why: The correct answer is: epitopes. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: Which class of molecules is the most antigenic?
why: The correct answer is: proteins. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

card.q: The variable regions of the heavy and light chains form the ________ sites of an antibody.

q: MHC I molecules present
why: The correct answer is: processed self-antigens from proteasomes.. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: MHC II molecules present
why: The correct answer is: processed foreign antigens from phagolysosomes.. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: Which type of antigen-presenting molecule is found on all nucleated cells?
why: The correct answer is: MHC I. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: Which type of antigen-presenting molecule is found only on macrophages, dendritic cells, and B cells?
why: The correct answer is: MHC II. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

card.q: MHC molecules are used for antigen ________ to T cells.
MHC II molecules are made up of two subunits (α and β) of approximately equal size, whereas MHC I molecules consist of a larger α subunit and a smaller subunit called ________.

q: What is a superantigen?
options: a protein that is highly efficient at stimulating a single type of productive and specific T cell response
a protein produced by antigen-presenting cells to enhance their presentation capabilities
a protein produced by T cells as a way of increasing the antigen activation they receive from antigen-presenting cells
a protein that activates T cells in a nonspecific and uncontrolled manner
why: The correct answer is: a protein that activates T cells in a nonspecific and uncontrolled manner. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: To what does the TCR of a helper T cell bind?
options: antigens presented with MHC I molecules
antigens presented with MHC II molecules
free antigen in a soluble form
why: The correct answer is: antigens presented with MHC II molecules. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: Cytotoxic T cells will bind with their TCR to which of the following?
options: antigens presented with MHC I molecules
antigens presented with MHC II molecules
free antigen in a soluble form
why: The correct answer is: antigens presented with MHC I molecules. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: A ________ molecule is a glycoprotein used to identify and distinguish white blood cells.
why: The correct answer is: cluster of differentiation. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: Name the T helper cell subset involved in antibody production.
why: The correct answer is: T_H2. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

card.q: A ________ T cell will become activated by presentation of foreign antigen associated with an MHC I molecule.

q: Which of the following would be a T-dependent antigen?
why: The correct answer is: protein. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: Which of the following would be a BCR?
why: The correct answer is: IgD. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: Which of the following does not occur during the lag period of the primary antibody response?
options: presentation of antigen with MHC II
why: The correct answer is: class switching to IgG. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

card.q: ________ antigens can stimulate B cells to become activated but require cytokine assistance delivered by helper T cells.

T-independent antigens can stimulate B cells to become activated and secrete antibodies without assistance from helper T cells. These antigens possess ________ antigenic epitopes that cross-link BCRs.

q: A patient is bitten by a dog with confirmed rabies infection. After treating the bite wound, the physician injects the patient with antibodies that are specific for the rabies virus to prevent the development of an active infection. This is an example of:
why: The correct answer is: Artificial passive immunity. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: A patient gets a cold, and recovers a few days later. The patient's classmates come down with the same cold roughly a week later, but the original patient does not get the same cold again. This is an example of:
why: The correct answer is: Natural active immunity. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

card.q: A(n) ________ pathogen is in a weakened state; it is still capable of stimulating an immune response but does not cause a disease.
________ immunity occurs when antibodies from one individual are harvested and given to another to protect against disease or treat active disease.
In the practice of ________, scabs from smallpox victims were used to immunize susceptible individuals against smallpox.

q: Which of the following is the type of cell largely responsible for type I hypersensitivity responses?
why: The correct answer is: mast cell. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: Type I hypersensitivities require which of the following initial priming events to occur?
why: The correct answer is: sensitization. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: Which of the following are the main mediators/initiators of type II hypersensitivity reactions?
why: The correct answer is: antibodies. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: Inflammatory molecules are released by mast cells in type I hypersensitivities; type II hypersensitivities, however, are characterized by which of the following?
options: localized tissue reactions, such as hives
why: The correct answer is: cell lysis (cytotoxicity). Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: An immune complex is an aggregate of which of the following?
why: The correct answer is: antibody and antigen molecules. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: Which of the following is a common treatment for type III hypersensitivity reactions?
why: The correct answer is: anti-inflammatory steroid treatments. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: Which of the following induces a type III hypersensitivity?
options: release of inflammatory molecules from mast cells
accumulation of immune complexes in tissues and small blood vessels
destruction of cells bound by antigens
destruction of cells bound by antibodies
why: The correct answer is: accumulation of immune complexes in tissues and small blood vessels. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: Which one of the following is not an example of a type IV hypersensitivity?
options: Contact dermatitis (e.g., contact with poison ivy)
why: The correct answer is: hemolytic disease of the newborn. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: Which of the following is an example of an organ-specific autoimmune disease?
why: The correct answer is: Addison disease. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: Which of the following is an example of a systemic autoimmune disease?
why: The correct answer is: myasthenia gravis. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

card.q: The thyroid-stimulating immunoglobulin that acts like thyroid-stimulating hormone and causes Graves disease is an antibody to the ________.

Match the graft with its description. ___autograft A. donor is a different species than the recipient ___allograft B. donor and recipient are the same individual ___xenograft C. donor is an identical twin of the recipient ___isograft D. donor is the same species as the recipient, but genetically different
Because it is a “transplant” that can include APCs and T cells from the donor, a bone marrow transplant may induce a very specific type of rejection known as ________ disease.

q: Which of the following is a genetic disease that results in lack of production of antibodies?
why: The correct answer is: agammaglobulinemia. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: Which of the following is a genetic disease that results in almost no adaptive immunity due to lack of B and/ or T cells?
why: The correct answer is: severe combined immunodeficiency. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: All but which one of the following are examples of secondary immunodeficiencies?
why: The correct answer is: chronic granulomatous disease. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: Cancer results when a mutation leads to which of the following?
why: The correct answer is: loss of cell-cycle control. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: Tumor antigens are ________ that are inappropriately expressed and found on abnormal cells.
why: The correct answer is: self antigens. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

card.q: A ________ cancer vaccine is one that stops the disease from occurring in the first place.
A ________ cancer vaccine is one that will help to treat the disease after it has occurred.

q: For many uses in the laboratory, polyclonal antibodies work well, but for some types of assays, they lack sufficient ________ because they cross-react with inappropriate antigens.
why: The correct answer is: specificity. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: How are monoclonal antibodies produced?
options: Antibody-producing B cells from a mouse are fused with myeloma cells and then the cells are grown in tissue culture.
A mouse is injected with an antigen and then antibodies are harvested from its serum.
They are produced by the human immune system as a natural response to an infection.
They are produced by a mouse’s immune system as a natural response to an infection.
why: The correct answer is: Antibody-producing B cells from a mouse are fused with myeloma cells and then the cells are grown in tissue culture.. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

card.q: When we inject an animal with the same antigen a second time a few weeks after the first, ________ takes place, which means the antibodies produced after the second injection will on average bind the antigen more tightly.
When using mAbs to treat disease in humans, the mAbs must first be ________ by replacing the mouse constant region DNA with human constant region DNA.
If we used normal mouse mAbs to treat human disease, multiple doses would cause the patient to respond with ________ against the mouse antibodies.

q: The formation of ________ is a positive result in the VDRL test.
why: The correct answer is: flocculant. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: The titer of a virus neutralization test is the highest dilution of patient serum
options: in which there is no detectable viral DNA.
in which there is no detectable viral protein.
that reduces plaque formation by at least 50%.
why: The correct answer is: that reduces plaque formation by at least 50%.. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: In the Ouchterlony assay, we see a sharp precipitin arc form between antigen and antiserum. Why does this arc remain visible for a long time?
options: The antibody molecules are too large to diffuse through the agar.
The precipitin lattice is too large to diffuse through the agar.
Methanol, added once the arc forms, denatures the protein and blocks diffusion.
The antigen molecules are chemically coupled to the gel matrix.
why: The correct answer is: The precipitin lattice is too large to diffuse through the agar.. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

card.q: When slowly adding antigen to an antiserum, the amount of precipitin would gradually increase until reaching the ________; addition of more antigen after this point would actually decrease the amount of precipitin.
card.a: equivalence zone or zone of equivalence

card.q: The radial immunodiffusion test quantifies antigen by mixing ________ into a gel and then allowing antigen to diffuse out from a well cut in the gel.

q: We use antisera to distinguish between various ________ within a species of bacteria.
why: The correct answer is: serovars. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: When using antisera to characterize bacteria, we will often link the antibodies to ________ to better visualize the agglutination.
why: The correct answer is: latex beads. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: The antibody screening test that is done along with pretransfusion blood typing is used to ensure that the recipient
options: does not have a previously undetected bacterial or viral infection.
actually does have the blood type stated in the online chart.
is not making antibodies against antigens outside the ABO or Rh systems.
why: The correct answer is: is not making antibodies against antigens outside the ABO or Rh systems.. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: The direct Coombs’ test is designed to detect when people have a disease that causes them to
options: make too many red blood cells.
produce antibodies that bind to their own red blood cells.
why: The correct answer is: produce antibodies that bind to their own red blood cells.. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: Viral hemagglutination assays only work with certain types of viruses because
options: the virus must be able to cross-link red blood cells directly.
the virus must be able to lyse red blood cells.
the virus must not be able to lyse red blood cells.
other viruses are too dangerous to work with in a clinical lab setting.
why: The correct answer is: the virus must be able to cross-link red blood cells directly.. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

card.q: In the major cross-match, we mix ________ with the donor red blood cells and look for agglutination.
Coombs’ reagent is an antiserum with antibodies that bind to human ________.

q: In an enzyme immunoassay, the enzyme
options: is bound by the antibody’s antigen-binding site.
is attached to the well of a microtiter plate.
is conjugated to the suspect antigen.
is bound to the constant region of the secondary antibody.
why: The correct answer is: is bound to the constant region of the secondary antibody.. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: When using an EIA to study microtubules or other structures inside a cell, we first chemically fix the cell and then treat the cells with alcohol. What is the purpose of this alcohol treatment?
options: It makes holes in the cell membrane large enough for antibodies to pass.
It makes the membrane sticky so antibodies will bind and be taken up by receptor-mediated endocytosis.
It removes negative charges from the membrane, which would otherwise repulse the antibodies.
It prevents nonspecific binding of the antibodies to the cell membrane.
why: The correct answer is: It makes holes in the cell membrane large enough for antibodies to pass.. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: In a lateral-flow pregnancy test, you see a blue band form on the control line and no band form on the test line. This is probably a ________ test for pregnancy.
why: The correct answer is: negative. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: When performing an FEIA, the fluorogen replaces the ________ that is used in an EIA.
why: The correct answer is: chromogenic substrate. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

card.q: To detect antibodies against bacteria in the bloodstream using an EIA, we would run a(n) ________, which we would start by attaching antigen from the bacteria to the wells of a microtiter plate.

q: Suppose you need to quantify the level of CD8 T cells in the blood of a patient recovering from influenza. options: There are no detectable CD8 cells.
There are three times as many CD4 cells than CD8 cells.
There are three times as many CD8 cells than CD4 cells.
CD8 cells make up about one-fourth of the total number of cells.
why: The correct answer is: CD8 cells make up about one-fourth of the total number of cells.. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: In the data described in the previous question, the average fluorescence intensity of cells in the second (red) peak is about ________ that in the first (blue) peak.
why: The correct answer is: 100 times. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: In a direct fluorescent antibody test, which of the following would we most likely be looking for using a fluorescently-labeled mAb?
options: bacteria isolated from a patient and grown on agar plates
antiserum from a patient smeared onto a glass slide
antiserum from a patient that had bound to antigen-coated beads
why: The correct answer is: bacteria in a patient sample. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

card.q: Fluorescence in a flow cytometer is measured by a detector set at an angle to the light source. There is also an in-line detector that can detect cell clumps or ________.

q: _____________ glands produce a lipid-rich substance that contains proteins and minerals and protects the skin.
why: The correct answer is: Sebaceous. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: Which layer of skin contains living cells, is vascularized, and lies directly above the hypodermis?
why: The correct answer is: the dermis. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

card.q: The ________ is the outermost layer of the epidermis.
The mucous membrane that covers the surface of the eyeball and inner eyelid is called the ________.

q: Staphylococcus aureus is most often associated with being
why: The correct answer is: coagulase-positive.. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: M protein is produced by
why: The correct answer is: Streptococcus pyogenes. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: ___________ is a major cause of preventable blindness that can be reduced through improved sanitation.
why: The correct answer is: Trachoma. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: Which species is frequently associated with nosocomial infections transmitted via medical devices inserted into the body?
why: The correct answer is: Staphylococcus epidermidis. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: Warts are caused by
why: The correct answer is: human papillomavirus.. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: Which of these viruses can spread to the eye to cause a form of keratitis?
why: The correct answer is: herpes simplex virus 1. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: Cold sores are associated with:
why: The correct answer is: herpes simplex viruses. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: Which disease is usually self-limiting but is most commonly treated with ganciclovir if medical treatment is needed?
why: The correct answer is: roseola. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: Adenoviruses can cause:
why: The correct answer is: viral conjunctivitis. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: ___________ is a superficial fungal infection found on the head.
why: The correct answer is: Tinea capitis. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: For what purpose would a health-care professional use a Wood’s lamp for a suspected case of ringworm?
options: to prevent the rash from spreading
why: The correct answer is: to visualize the fungus. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: Sabouraud dextrose agar CC is selective for:
why: The correct answer is: non-saprophytic fungi. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: The first-line recommended treatment for sporotrichosis is:
why: The correct answer is: itraconazole. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

card.q: The most common subcutaneous mycosis in temperate regions is ________.

q: Which of the following is most likely to cause an Acanthamoeba infection?
options: swimming in a lake while wearing contact lenses
being bitten by deerflies in Central Africa
living environments in a college dormitory with communal showers
participating in a contact sport such as wrestling
why: The correct answer is: swimming in a lake while wearing contact lenses. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: The parasitic Loa loa worm can cause great pain when it:
options: exits through the skin of the foot
why: The correct answer is: travels through the conjunctiva. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: A patient tests positive for Loa loa antibodies. What does this test indicate?
options: The individual was exposed to Loa loa at some point.
The individual is currently suffering from loiasis.
The individual has never been exposed to Loa loa.
why: The correct answer is: The individual was exposed to Loa loa at some point.. Re-read the lesson above to see why.
